ANSWER OF  
ALLEGHENY ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. 
TO SHOW CAUSE ORDER  
ISSUED IN CONNECTION WITH THE TREATMENT OF  
CO-LOCATED LOAD WITHIN PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C.  
 
 
Allegheny Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“Allegheny”) respectfully tenders for filing to the 
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) this Answer in the above-
captioned proceeding concerning the treatment of large loads located at the same site as 
generating facilities (“Co-Located Load”) within the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) 
footprint.  Allegheny submits this Answer pursuant to Rule 213 of the FERC Rules of Practice 
and Procedure1 and the Commission’s February 20, 2025 Order Instituting Proceeding Under 
Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other Proceedings (“Show Cause 
Order”).2  The Show Cause Order directs PJM as well as each of the PJM Transmission Owners 
(“TOs”) to address the treatment of Co-Located Load by PJM’s Open Access Transmission 
 
1   18 C.F.R. § 385.213. 
2   PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,195 (2025).

2 
 
Tariff, the Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of PJM, and the Reliability Assurance 
Agreement Among Load Serving Entities in the PJM Region (collectively, “PJM Tariff”).  
Specifically, the Show Cause Order directs PJM and the TOs to either (1) show cause that the 
PJM Tariff remains just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential without 
rates, terms, and conditions of service specific to Co-Located Load or (2) explain what changes 
to the Tariff would be necessary to address Co-Located Load.  In the Answer below, Allegheny 
acknowledges both the growth of interest in Co-Located Load and the importance of clarity in 
transmission rate and policies as to the treatment of Co-Located Load within the PJM Tariff.  
The Show Cause Order is the culmination of a number of contentious proceedings before 
the Commission addressing issues related to Co-Located Load.  In these proceedings, market 
participants have espoused a number of views as to (1) whether specific configurations of Co-
Located Load may sufficiently sever itself from the transmission grid such that it receives no 
benefits from the grid, (2) whether Co-Located Load should be assessed transmission charges, 
(3) what rates, terms, and conditions of transmission service would encourage or discourage Co-
Located Load, and (4) whether the PJM Tariff should be revised to accommodate Co-Located 
Load.  Allegheny itself has taken no position on these questions, and it remains uncommitted as 
to whether the current PJM Tariff sufficiently addresses Co-Located Load and the more 
fundamental question of whether Co-Located Load should be allocated transmission costs.  
Ultimately, by the conclusion of this proceeding, the Commission will have a substantial record 
on which to determine whether to direct revisions to the PJM Tariff to accommodate Co-Located 
Load.  With the voluminous record in the consolidated proceedings and the burgeoning number 
of proceedings related to the issue of Co-Located Load, Allegheny is certain that the need for 
clarity from the Commission is both essential and urgent.

3 
 
 
I.  
PRELIMINARY STATEMENT 
 
This Answer is submitted pursuant to Rule 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of 
the Commission and the Commission’s February 20, 2025 Show Cause Order, which established 
March 24, 2025 as the date by which PJM and the TOs are required to submit answers in this 
Section 206 proceeding. 
II. 
DESCRIPTION OF ALLEGHENY 
Allegheny is a non-profit electric generation and transmission cooperative corporation 
(“G&T Cooperative”), incorporated under the Electric Cooperative Law of the Commonwealth 
of Pennsylvania, and it is the exclusive wholesale supplier of its 14 distribution cooperative 
members.  Similar to other G&T Cooperatives, Allegheny is owned entirely by its members.  Its 
Board of Directors, which governs Allegheny, is comprised exclusively of representatives of 
each of its members.  Thirteen of Allegheny’s members are located in Pennsylvania, and one is 
located in New Jersey.  Allegheny provides service to its members, which in turn serve over 
600,000 rural consumer-members in Pennsylvania and New Jersey.   
Allegheny is a PJM TO with transmission facilities included in the PPL Zone, the zone 
which also includes PPL’s transmission facilities.  Allegheny serves load in five PJM zones:  the 
PPL Zone, the Allegheny Power Zone, the Penelec Zone, the Met-Ed Zone, and the JCP&L 
Zone.  Allegheny is a ten-percent co-owner and Nuclear Regulatory Commission co-licensee of 
the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station, an approximately 2,600 megawatt, two-unit nuclear 
power plant located in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania.

4 
 
III. 
BACKGROUND 
The Commission has addressed issues related to Co-Located Load within PJM in a 
number of recent proceedings. 
In Docket No. ER24-2172, the Commission considered amendments to a non-conforming 
Interconnection Service Agreement (“ISA”) among PJM, Susquehanna Nuclear, LLC and PPL 
Electric Utilities Corporation that would have increased the amount of Co-Located Load at the 
Susquehanna Steam Electric Station from 300 MW to 480 MW.  The proceeding attracted over 
60 intervenors and drew comments from industry participants throughout the nation, weighing in 
on the questions raised in the opening paragraphs of this Answer.  On November 1, 2024, the 
Commission rejected the proposed amendments to the ISA, finding that PJM had failed to meet 
the burden of demonstrating that the non-conforming provisions of the ISA were necessary.3  In 
particular, the Commission stated that the proceeding raised questions as to whether PJM would 
offer the same terms and conditions of service to similarly situated Co-Located Load 
interconnection customers.4   
In Docket Nos. ER24-2888 et al., on August 28, 2024, several subsidiaries of Exelon 
Company submitted for Commission approval proposed revisions to their respective 
transmission rate schedules contained in Attachment H of the PJM Open Access Transmission 
Tariff to address Co-Located Load.  Specifically, the Exelon Company subsidiaries proposed to 
revise their transmission rate schedules to clarify that Co-Located Load must be designated as 
either Network Load or receive Point-to-Point Transmission Service and thus be allocated costs 
of the transmission grid.  On February 20, 2025, the Commission issued an order rejecting the 
 
3  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,078, at P 87 (2024). 
4  
Id.

5 
 
Exelon Company subsidiaries’ proposal as outside the scope of rights afforded to PJM TOs by 
the PJM Tariff.5      
In Docket No. AD24-11, the Commission convened a technical conference on November 
1, 2024 to examine technical, legal, and policy issues in connection with Co-Located Loads.  It 
subsequently issued a notice requesting post-technical conference comments.   
In Docket No. EL25-20, Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) filed a 
complaint with the Commission on November 22, 2024, arguing that the PJM Tariff is unjust 
and unreasonable for failing to contain rules for interconnection customers to follow when 
seeking a Co-Located Load configuration that is fully isolated from the transmission grid.   
In Docket No. EL25-49, the Commission issued the February 20, 2025 Show Cause 
Order to which Allegheny now responds.  In initiating this Federal Power Act Section 206 
proceeding, the Commission also consolidated this investigation with the Constellation 
complaint proceeding in Docket No. EL25-20 and the inquiry it launched in Docket No. AD24-
11 to examine the technical, legal, and policy implications presented by Co-Located Load.  
IV. 
ANSWER 
Electricity and capacity markets are in a state of flux as the nation experiences  
unprecedented load growth forecasts for the first time in decades.  This load growth is driven by 
increased electrification including the embrace of electric vehicles,6 considerable manufacturing 
investments spurred by federal legislation,7 and perhaps most prominently the advancement of 
 
5  
Atlantic City Elec. Co., 190 FERC ¶ 61,109 (2025). 
6  
Erik Delarue & KU Leuven, Load Electrification Impact, ENERGY SYSTEMS INTEGRATION GROUP (Nov. 25, 
2024), www.esig.energy/load-electification-impact (last visited Mar. 18, 2025). 
7  
Brad Plumer & Nadja Popovich, A New Surge in Power Use is Threatening U.S. Climate Goals, N.Y. TIMES 
(Mar. 14, 2024), available at https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/03/13/climate/electric-power-climate-
change.html (last visited Mar. 18, 2025).

6 
 
artificial intelligence (“AI”) and data center development.8  Increasingly, large load is looking to 
secure a dedicated source of generation as a means of ensuring both reliability and affordability.  
Accordingly, Co-Located Load configurations are attractive options to many new large loads.   
As demonstrated both by the litany of FERC proceedings identified above and the 
substantial number of intervenors in those FERC proceedings, the issue of the appropriate 
treatment of Co-Located Load has perplexed industry.  Yet, foundational, but ultimately 
technical, questions remain unanswered:  Does Co-Located Load sited with generation that is 
interconnected to the transmission grid benefit from the generator’s interconnection to the 
transmission grid?  What, if any, transmission services does Co-Located Load receive from the 
transmission grid under the various configuration models?  Can Co-Located Load ever 
sufficiently sever itself from the transmission grid so as not benefit from the transmission grid?    
Sophisticated technical experts and market participants have weighed the evidence in the FERC 
proceedings identified above and have reached entirely conflicting answers to these questions.   
In this proceeding, the Commission must layer legal and policy considerations atop the 
technical questions identified above.  Thus, it is important to recognize that the Commission is 
presented with these technical questions regarding the interconnection of new large loads at the 
same time that the industry is grappling with a dearth of capacity and, more broadly, ever-
increasing transmission costs.  The loss of large baseload generation is having real-world impacts 
for load-serving entities.  As one example, in PJM, the 2025/2026 Base Residual Auction 
(“BRA”) produced a capacity auction clearing price nearly ten times that of the 2024/2025 
 
8  
DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, 2024 UNITED STATES DATA CENTER ENERGY USAGE REPORT (Dec. 2024), available 
at https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-releases-new-report-evaluating-increase-electricity-demand-data-centers 
(last visited Mar. 18, 2025).

7 
 
BRA.9  One of many converging factors that produced an increase of this magnitude is the fact 
that supply offered into the capacity market declined by nearly 9% from the 2024/2025 BRA to 
the 2025/2026 BRA.10  Escalating capacity prices is one symptom of a lack of sufficient 
generation resources to meet needs, but a far more significant concern is the ability to meet 
existing service obligations.  This concern was highlighted by the December 9, 2024 warning 
issued by PJM Board Chair Mark Takahashi that a capacity shortage may affect the PJM system 
as early as the 2026/2027 Delivery Year.11  Additionally, the lack of generation capacity has a 
direct impact on transmission prices as well because, as baseload generation resources retire, grid 
operators must approve additional and more costly transmission projects to serve existing load.  
For example, in February 2025, PJM approved a new Regional Transmission Expansion Plan 
(“RTEP”) that included costly transmission projects necessitated by generation retirements, 
including one project whose costs more than doubled from the prior RTEP.12   
Because certain Co-Located Load configurations may eliminate an existing resource from 
the capacity market and potentially exempt Co-Located Load from transmission charges, a legal 
and policy question that the Commission must address in this proceeding is whether Co-Located

(documenting the increase in the clearing price from $28.92 in the 2024/2025 Base Residual Auction to $269.92 
in the 2025/2026 Base Residual Auction).    
10  Id. at 3.   
11  Letter from Mark Takahashi, Chair, Board of Managers, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., to Stakeholders (Dec. 9, 
2024), available at https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-
disclosures/2024/20241209-board-letter-outlining-action-on-capacity-market-adjustments-rri-and-sis.pdf (last 
checked Mar. 19, 2025). 
12  Ethan Howland, PJM Board Approves $6.7B Transmission Expansion Plan, Utility Drive, Feb. 27, 2025, 
available at https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-rtep-transmission-expansion-plan-aep-dominion-
firstenergy/741097 (last checked Mar. 20, 2025); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Transmission Expansion 
Advisory Committee (TEAC) Recommendations to the PJM Board at 4-5 (Feb. 2005) (identifying the costs of 
the transmission projects designed to ameliorate reliability issues associated with the retirement of the Brandon 
Shores coal-fired power project).

8 
 
Load configurations will exacerbate current strains on the transmission system, potentially 
impairing reliability and increasing capacity and transmission costs to ratepayers.  Allegheny 
does not oppose Co-Located Load configurations but insists that the interconnection and 
treatment of Co-Located Load be accomplished in a manner that is fair to existing load and 
adheres rigidly to the Commission’s long-standing cost causation principle.  In short, if Co-
Located Load benefits from the transmission system, it must be allocated the costs of those 
benefits to ensure that all users of the transmission system pay their fair share of the costs of 
maintaining and expanding the transmission system.    
Ultimately, resolutions of the technical questions identified above will assist the 
Commission in answering the legal and policy questions presented by Co-Located Load.  With 
the record to be produced in response to the Show Cause Order, combined with the record in the 
Constellation complaint proceeding and in the FERC-convened technical conference, the 
Commission will be well-positioned to respond to an industry that is clamoring for certainty.  
Though a party to many of the proceedings identified above, Allegheny has taken no position on 
the foundational technical questions at issue in this proceeding related to whether Co-Located 
Load benefits from the transmission grid.  The Commission should make its determinations in 
this proceeding based on the record evidence as to technical, legal, and policy implications of 
interconnecting Co-Located Load.  Because Allegheny has no direct experience with 
interconnecting Co-Located Load, it respectfully defers to the findings of the Commission on 
these important questions but asks that the Commission act with expediency for the benefit of 
owners and users of the PJM transmission system, ensuring adherence to the Commission’s long-
standing cost causation principle and keeping in mind that load-serving entities rely on the PJM 
transmission system to provide reliable and affordable service.

9 
 
V. 
RESERVATION OF RIGHTS 
Allegheny reserves the right to posit and address any issues that it or others may identify 
or raise herein that are developed in any other phase of this proceeding. 
VI.  
CONCLUSION 
The present proceeding presents the Commission with many legal and policy 
questions that should be answered by a robust review of the technical aspects of Co-
Located Load.  Answering these questions is necessary to provide clarity to ensure that 
the United States retains technology-driven large load, including those related to data 
centers and AI, that is capable of locating elsewhere but is important for national security.  
Most importantly, resolving these outstanding questions will provide clarity to load-
serving entities as to how they will meet their existing load obligations reliably and 
affordably at a time of diminishing generation resources.  Allegheny supports the 
Commission’s efforts to provide certainty on an expedited basis to the questions posed by the 
growth of Co-Located Load configurations in the PJM region.   
 
Dated:  March 24, 2025 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,
